‘What, me worry?’ Yes, if you’re paying attention to threats surrounding the midterms.
President Donald Trump speaks during an Oct. 19, 2026, rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas (Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector).
As the November midterm elections draw near, much of the nation seemingly has channeled Mad Magazine’s smiling, redheaded, gap-toothed mascot Alfred E. Neuman and his catchphrase: “What, me worry?” But the nation has plenty to worry about.
Here’s what the current administration has done in the months leading up to November’s white-knuckle vote.
This administration has purged “disloyal” federal workers and pardoned convicted Jan. 6, 2021, rioters who attacked police at the U.S. Capitol. Trump has dumped billions of dollars into beefing up the ranks of heavily armed, masked loyalists now roaming American cities.
His Supreme Court has gutted the Voting Rights Act, which led some formerly Confederate states into racial gerrymanders disguised as partisan gerrymanders. It also has expanded the power of the presidency and weakened our system of checks and balances.
Trump encouraged a mid-decade redistricting push intended to give Republicans an electoral advantage. Redistricting typically occurs every 10 years.
For the first time in more than two decades, the United State has blocked international election observers from monitoring our elections. Amid claims of widespread voter fraud (nearly nonexistent in reality), the president plans to blanket polling places with a network of federal election monitors.
Trump fired the leaders of the U.S. Election Assistance Commission in July, leaving the EAC without any sitting commissioners. A Supreme Court decision expanded the president’s authority to fire members of independent agencies. Commissioners had resisted his push for proof of U.S. citizenship in voter registration. The bipartisan commission certified voting systems, distributed federal election grants and maintained the national mail-in voter form.
He also has continued his claims that voting machines remain vulnerable to manipulation and that his political opponents stole the 2020 election. Fears linger about armed ICE agents appearing in and around polling places. He has until recently discouraged mail-in voting.
This administration has imprisoned people in El Salvador and bombed boats suspected of drug smuggling without due process.
The president’s party has abdicated its role as a check on the power of the executive branch.
Trump sent Tulsi Gabbard into a Georgia election office and confiscated ballots. This after calling that state’s election official and asking the man to “find” more than 11,000 votes. Recent national elections have run so close that a campaign only would need to nudge the needle 2 or 3 percentage points to swing the election.
Despite all this, an eerie silence on what this behavior portends has settled over the nation. Few if any people seem alarmed.
The president has said unless he wins, the elections are rigged.
Alfred E. Neuman would not be smiling. He’d be worried.
Here in Kansas, civic rights organizations have begun ramping up voting integrity efforts in preparation for these threats.

I’ve always been more of an anaerobic athlete, meaning I love shorter, faster running and strength workouts. In fact, I love strength so much that even during my first marathon training block, I enthusiastically committed to three heavy lifts a week.
While strength training prevents injuries, makes you more durable, and can even boost your running economy, says Des Clarke, an RRCA-certified run coach based in Phoenix, I often spent evenings in the gym lifting weights instead of allowing my body to recover from 40-mile weeks.
As I started training for a half marathon for the second time, I decided to put more of an emphasis on mileage. I didn’t want to nix strength from my schedule entirely, but I had to figure out how to dial back my time with the weights and increase my running time in a safe, balanced way.
Doing so helped me run a 1:46:50 half marathon on a majorly hilly course. Here’s what I did to get there so you can strike a better balance, too.
How I Increased My Mileage Safely Without Sacrificing Strength
For anyone running half marathons and marathons (especially someone who’s newer to longer distances like I am), higher mileage weeks give you the base you need to run longer and faster.
“If you want to get better at running, it is true that to a point, you need to run more,” says Clarke. “You’re building the aerobic capacity, strength, and durability that you need to run those distances without getting injured.” That looks like building volume incrementally over time, she says.
Before I started half marathon training, I was running at least two times each week for about eight months. I was pretty consistent, but knew I could afford to add more miles. So before starting my plan, I added another day of running to my schedule, and then when I kicked off the first week, I tackled four days a week of running.
I also added some more miles to my midweek runs. Last training cycle, I usually opted for four-milers, but this time, I bumped it up to five or six miles.
Clarke typically recommends repeating the same weekly mileage for two to three weeks in a row to make sure an athlete has adapted to that particular load before increasing again. I did this during several weeks of my plan.
In that same vein, it’s useful to take a deload week every three weeks or so to better absorb training gains, Clarke says. This involves scaling back your mileage by around 10 to 20 percent before returning to your typical volume. My training plan also included these, allowing me recovery time while pushing mileage.
To balance this increase in mileage, I dropped to two lifting days per week instead of three, cutting down on volume (and consequently my overall time spent in the gym), which Clarke recommends. Last year during marathon training, I spent three days a week lifting weights for about an hour or more. This training cycle, I’ve spent 30 to 45 minutes lifting weights one to two times a week. I split up my usual hour-long routine into two separate days and alternated between them.
How Swapping Strength Training for More Miles Paid Off
1. I Actually Felt Recovered Going Into Every Run
I remember how exhausting it felt to spend more than four hours a week strength training on top of 35- to 40-mile weeks during marathon training. Cutting my time in the weight room in half each week (from three hour-long lifts to two 45-minute lifts) not only allowed me to fit in a few extra miles but take my recovery more seriously, too.

The artificial intelligence (AI) investing thesis has been tough during the past month, but a bundle of tech earnings can change sentiment. Alphabet (GOOG -1.08%) (GOOGL -1.24%), Microsoft (MSFT +0.66%), and Amazon (AMZN -0.95%) are some of the tech giants slated to report earnings by the end of the month, and these are the key details every investor should monitor.
AI capital expenditures
If hyperscalers say that they will continue to ramp up spending, it gives chipmakers, neoclouds, and other companies at the center of the AI trade full permission to rebound.
Elon Musk offered some good news when SpaceX (SPCX +1.89%) reported earnings earlier this month. He told investors that hyperscalers and AI enterprises have been relentlessly "hound[ing]" SpaceX for more compute. Even SpaceX is struggling to find compute, with Musk expecting the superintelligence computing capacity shortage to last for years.
That backdrop suggests hyperscalers will spend more than expected and project even higher AI capital expenditures into the fourth quarter and beyond.
That would be good news, but it's equally important to assess how each company will fund its capital expenditures. Microsoft already told investors it would achieve positive free cash flow in its fiscal 2027, suggesting that the AI build-out is sustainable.
Revenue growth rates
All this spending has to translate into positive returns to justify the huge cost of the AI build-out. That's why investors should closely look at year-over-year growth rates for the tech giants. It's already clear that chipmakers are still doing well. Micron (MU +2.46%) posted 379% year-over-year revenue growth in its fiscal Q4 2026 as demand for its memory chips continues to soar.
However, all those chips have to translate into meaningful revenue growth rates for hyperscalers to justify the increased capital expenditures. Alphabet's cloud revenue, specifically, will be on my radar. That part of the business has been accelerating a lot lately, including an 82% year-over-year growth rate in the second quarter. The more Google Cloud's revenue growth rate accelerates in the third quarter, the better it is for the AI trade.

Profitability also matters, but there are two reasons I am not looking at net income as much. First, it's normal for tech innovations to be unprofitable for multiple years before enjoying dramatic profit margin expansion upon profitability. Google Cloud is a great example, since it was unprofitable for more than a decade.
Second, net income has been murky for some tech giants due to their large investments in SpaceX and Anthropic. Returns from those investments influence net income, but don't indicate how well the underlying businesses are actually doing. For this earnings cycle, operating income is a more reliable metric than net income, because the former isn't affected by large investments that are performing well for now.
Forward guidance
Chipmakers have offered forward guidance that implies demand will continue. The projections from tech giants will suggest how they feel about current AI expenditures, and whether it is translating into higher growth rates.
Commentary from tech leaders will also reveal where they see AI heading. For instance, Amazon Chief Executive Officer Andy Jassy told investors that Amazon Web Services was booming in Q2, and that "there's a lot to be excited about."

The $500 Billion Question: Can Google Cloud’s Massive AI Backlog Outrun Its Mind-Boggling CapEx Boom on Oct. 28?
Google Cloud's backlog just crossed $500 billion while free cash flow turned negative for the first time ever, and Wednesday's earnings report will reveal whether Alphabet's historic spending spree is pulling ahead of its own ability to pay for it.
Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL | GOOGL Price Prediction, NASDAQ:GOOG) reports third-quarter results after the close on Wednesday, October 28. Google Cloud’s backlog stands at $514 billion, and 2026 CapEx guidance runs $195 billion to $205 billion. This report shows which one is growing faster.
Record Cloud Growth Meets Negative Free Cash Flow
Last quarter, revenue rose 24.2% to $119.80 billion, ahead of the $116.91 billion consensus. Google Cloud led again. Revenue there rose 82% to $24.77 billion, speeding up from 63% in Q1 and 34% a year ago, while Cloud operating margin expanded to 35.6% from 20.7%.
Costs grew just as fast. CapEx rose 100% to $44.92 billion, free cash flow came in at negative $5.86 billion — the first time ever — and management raised its 2026 CapEx range from $180 billion to $190 billion. To pay for it, Alphabet raised about $70 billion in equity and debt and suspended buybacks.
Reported EPS of $9.11 included a $99.03 billion equity securities gain, yet shares fell 6.89% on the day of the report. GOOG closed Friday at $317.28, down 5.83% over the past week.
Consensus Calls for Nearly 25% Revenue Growth
The full-year EPS figure includes the first half’s equity gains, which makes the quarterly estimate the cleaner gauge of operating profit.
Backlog Conversion and Margins Will Set the Tone
My first focus will be the backlog. It rose by more than $50 billion sequentially last quarter, and management expects to recognize just over 50% of it within 24 months. Sundar Pichai said in July, “We are still in a supply-constrained environment.”
Margins come next. Alphabet planned to lean on third-party capacity in Q3 as a bridge, which management said would create “modest margin pressure,” on top of Wiz integration costs and rising depreciation. You should compare Cloud margin against 35.6% and consolidated operating margin against 34%.
On spending, any change to the 2026 range matters, as does early color on 2027, when management expects CapEx to “increase significantly.” TPU system sales add another variable. That revenue ramps as Alphabet leaves 2026, with the “vast majority” arriving in 2027.
All that CapEx has to be powered, cooled, and connected by somebody, which is the entire point of a free report we put together on seven AI infrastructure suppliers that aren’t the chipmakers: you can grab it here.
Search still has to fund the expansion. Revenue there grew 17% to $63.3 billion, and AI Mode passed 1 billion monthly users. A court has already rejected a forced breakup of Google’s ad-tech business, so any detail on the remaining behavioral remedies could also move opinion.
A $514 Billion Backlog Has to Turn Into Cash
Alphabet beat estimates in all 8 of its last reports. Even so, the stock’s moves on report day ranged from a 9.97% gain to a 6.89% drop, and the market now cares most about how efficiently that capital gets spent. If the backlog turns into revenue fast enough to steady free cash flow while CapEx keeps rising, the spending case gets easier to defend heading into a greater 2027.

Former CEO of Alphabet Inc.'s Google, Eric Schmidt, said China trails the U.S. in the AI race by roughly six months, but it could still be the winner.
In a podcast called In Good Company, hosted by Nicolai Tangen, CEO of Norges Bank Investment Management, on Wednesday, Schmidt said, "I don't know that they will get ahead, but I will tell you that…if they're six months behind, then we're already losing because their strategy is that the products are free."
Chinese AI models are often free or less expensive, potentially attracting consumers in developing economies that cannot afford costly, closed Western systems, he said. Open-weight models could further accelerate global use.
He credited China's progress partly to access to advanced chips he said were "not supposed to have" and were "pilfered or smuggled" into the country. He also cited distillation, in which developers query Western AI systems and train their own models using the responses.
Schmidt, who personally owns a stake in Anthropic, rejected comparisons between the AI industry and a speculative bubble. He pointed to Anthropic's revenue growth and paying customers as evidence of commercial demand. Schmidt said that Google set a revenue-growth record during his tenure as CEO, but Anthropic surpassed it by growing at more than twice the pace.
"That's real growth. It's not fake. It's real money, with real customers who are paying for something useful," he said.
AI's Price Tag: A Risk for US Big Tech?
Schmidt echoed IMD Business School professor Howard Yu, who told Benzinga that OpenAI and Anthropic's four-to-six-month lead over Chinese AI rivals could prove "very perishable," as many users do not need the most advanced models.
He cited Tencent Holdings Ltd's WeChat agent, which quickly generated personalized guidance by scanning medicine packaging, to illustrate how less sophisticated AI can deliver practical value. For businesses, he added, cost matters, with executives weighing AI spending against hiring more employees.
In June, Polsia AI CEO Ben Cera warned that cheaper Chinese open-source AI models like DeepSeek's R-1 model and Alibaba Group Holdings' Qwen3 and Qwen2.5 could undermine the business models and valuations of OpenAI and Anthropic by offering near-frontier capabilities at a fraction of the cost.
He argued that enterprises may no longer justify spending millions on AI when comparable alternatives cost far less, declaring, "The bubble isn't AI. It's the price of AI." Cera added that AI model-focused companies could face the biggest losses, while hyperscalers such as Alphabet may be better positioned to weather the shift.

Investing.com -- Goldman Sachs has cut its 12-month target for South Korea's Kospi Index by 25%, citing mounting concerns over artificial intelligence investments and more conservative equity valuations.
Strategists led by Timothy Moe lowered their target to 9,000 from 12,000 after the benchmark plunged more than 35% from its June peak.
Despite the downgrade, the revised forecast still implies upside of more than 60% from current levels, reflecting the bank's view that Korean equities have become significantly undervalued.
The investment bank had previously raised its Kospi target in June and maintained its bullish outlook even as global technology stocks began retreating amid concerns about AI spending.
South Korea's market has been particularly vulnerable because of its heavy exposure to semiconductor manufacturers Samsung Electronics (KRX:005930) and SK Hynix (KRX:000660).
Both companies have benefited from demand for memory chips used in AI infrastructure, making the Kospi a major indicator of investor sentiment toward the technology.
However, concerns about rising financing costs, massive infrastructure investments and uncertain returns have triggered widespread selling across Korean equities.
Goldman's strategists said the market was pricing in an excessively pessimistic outlook for corporate fundamentals.
The Kospi's 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen to approximately four, a level not seen across 18 major markets since 2006.
Korean stocks now trade at roughly half the valuation of Indonesian equities, highlighting the scale of the recent selloff.
According to the bank's estimates, current semiconductor valuations imply a 65% decline in sector earnings in 2027, a scenario the strategists consider overly pessimistic.
Meanwhile, companies outside the memory chip sector, representing approximately half the Kospi, trade at 7.6 times forward earnings.
Despite lowering its overall market target, Goldman continues to favour opportunities in power, industrials, corporate governance-related stocks, and companies benefiting from domestic economic recovery and Korean popular culture.

In a report published on Oct. 19, JPMorgan's asset management arm projected 10% annualized returns on Bitcoin over the next 10 years. By comparison, it projected 5.5% for gold, 5.6% for Treasury bonds and 7.5% for large-cap equities.

JPMorgan's shift in tone is remarkable given the longstanding skepticism toward digital assets from its CEO Jamie Dimon. In 2017, he derided Bitcoin as a "fraud" heading toward a crash. He has kept up a barrage of criticism against Bitcoin, dismissing it as "a pet rock" and "worthless" over the years. Just last year, JPMorgan began allowing its clients to buy Bitcoin as banks developed a stronger interest in crypto.
"I don't think you should smoke, but I defend your right to smoke," Dimon said during JPMorgan's annual investor day in May 2025. "I defend your right to buy bitcoin."
However, the report offered a significant caveat for its projection: It still doesn't recommend Bitcoin as something that investors should purchase for a diversified portfolio.
Diving into JPMorgan's Bitcoin forecast
Bitcoin is a digital asset designed to be sent electronically between users anywhere in the world without a bank or government facilitating the transfer. Therefore, its value is not determined by a central government. It only stems from what an investor is prepared to pay. Bitcoin's volatility made JPMorgan analysts cautious about incorporating it in investment portfolios.
"At the moment, we do not make a case for bitcoin (BTC) as a diversifier in portfolios due to its unstable market correlations," JPMorgan analysts Sheena Shah and Dennis Cristallo wrote in the analysis. "We see bitcoin as a speculative asset and a hedge against monetary easing."

A procurement officer sits down on a Monday morning to build a budget for an enterprise AI agent rollout. They open eight browser tabs, one for each of the primary platforms: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, xAI, Meta, ServiceNow, and Salesforce. The goal is simple — find a per-seat or per-unit price to drop into a spreadsheet. By the time they reach the end of the list, no single metric has appeared that lets them compare one agent against another. What they have instead is a row of quote-gated portals, usage meters and third-party estimates: enough material to fill the spreadsheet, not enough to defend it.
Four of the eight publish no public enterprise-agent price on their own surface. OpenAI Presence lists no price on its product page or its announcement; the service is not self-serve, is limited to eligible enterprise customers, and routes buyers to contact sales or an account team — a quote-gated enterprise SKU, where the pricing mechanism exists and simply is not shown. Meta's Business Agent announcement says getting started is free and that paid subscription offerings are planned, but publishes no seat or subscription price. Meta's own developer documentation — which returned a 400 on direct fetch and reached us through an indexed snippet plus two independent third-party guides — carries the one Meta number that exists: $2.00 per 1 million tokens for Business Agent replies on the WhatsApp Business Platform, effective August 1, roughly four to five cents a message. The enterprise custom-agent platform stays unpublished. ServiceNow's AI agents page carries a "Contact us for a quote" call to action and the site has no official pricing page at all; third-party estimates put ITSM at $70 to $200+ per fulfiller per month, which are not ServiceNow figures. Google Gemini Enterprise closes the four: its official pricing surfaces display no per-seat dollar rate, and the $21-to-$60 range in circulation is third-party reported US list pricing, never confirmed on a current Google page.
The two that do publish hand you units that refuse to line up. Microsoft Copilot Studio sells a capacity pack of 25,000 Copilot Credits at $200.00 a month off a published rate card, alongside a pay-as-you-go meter through Azure. Microsoft has moved off the older model in which 25,000 messages cost $200, and because consumption now depends on how an agent is designed and used, a message no longer maps to a flat price. Salesforce Agentforce, whose pricing page was last modified October 19, publishes the fullest card in the group — Flex Credits at $500 per 100,000 credits with each Agentforce action drawing 20 of them, a $5 per-user license, a $125 add-on, a $150 industry add-on, a $50 Coworker license, a Max Edition from $550 — all of it off that page. It also shows $2 per conversation, except the card carrying that price now reads, to anyone arriving as a new buyer, "For existing Agentforce Conversations customers. Contact your Account Executive for more information." A published price, retired inside the page that still prints it. Credits, conversations, actions and seats do not convert into one another, which is why two vendors with honest rate cards still cannot be ranked against each other from public information — the problem four rival agents and the infrastructure pricing gap both already set

A typical marathon-training schedule involves several months of increasing mileage. But the physical gains you earn from all of those runs are only part of the equation that can make or break your race.
“As a coach, I always emphasize the importance of preparing for more than just the distance,” says Gab Reznik, NASM-certified personal trainer, run coach, and head coach at Tone House, a fitness studio in New York City. “Marathon training isn’t simply about building the fitness to cover 26.2 miles. It’s about developing the confidence, adaptability, and mental resilience to handle whatever challenges arise along the way.” Because if there’s one guarantee in the marathon, it’s that something unexpected will come your way.
To help you prepare for any scenario that pops up during your 26.2, we tapped three run coaches for their insights about what marathoners tend to report back to them postrace—the things that surprised them, the mindsets that helped them when the miles got grueling, and what they wish they’d known sooner to make the race go smoother.
Use this roundup of lessons they’ve learned along the way as your cheat sheet for a faster finish and more gratifying race day overall.
You might feel wiped out before the race even starts.
“One thing we’ve heard from several of our athletes after the marathon is how mentally exhausting the logistics of getting to the start can be; it’s a lot of hurry up and wait,” says Matt Wilpers, Peloton instructor and endurance coach. “You’re up early, navigating transportation, surrounded by thousands of other runners, and then sitting around in the athletes’ village waiting for your wave. By the time the race starts, you’ve already spent several hours managing logistics, anticipation, and nervous energy.”
This can be true regardless of your race, even if you’re not tackling one of the World Marathon Majors, but many of those races offer particularly difficult starts.
How to prep:
A little extra planning can help make all of those prerace moments feel more streamlined and less mentally taxing. Wilpers suggests treating the hours before the start as part of your race plan. “Know your transportation options, anticipate the waiting, bring food and extra layers, and eliminate as many uncertainties as possible,” he says. “The more decisions you make in advance, the more energy and attention you’ll have available when it matters most.”
Reznik also advises packing a portable charger, which is especially wise for big races, as the athletes’ village and start line at those often have bad cell service. “The last thing you want is to arrive at the starting line with a dead phone,” she says.
It’s way too easy to start out way too fast.
Getting caught up in the excitement early on in a race is natural, and “it’s easy to let that excitement dictate your pace,” says Reznik. If there’s any decline in the opening sections of your marathon (like the second mile of the NYC Marathon), it tends to be that much more difficult to restrain yourself and settle into a controlled rhythm.
How to prep:
Plan to begin slightly slower than your goal pace, advises Wilpers, and allow yourself to warm up when you’re in the race rather than forcing the pace from the beginning. “From there, the goal is to gradually settle into a rhythm and put yourself in a position to finish strong,” he says.
Practicing holding back during long training runs will help it feel natural on race day and not leave you anxious about getting behind on your goal

Ann Chisholm, owner and coach at Tropos Fitness Club in Victoria, British Columbia, stands before a crowd of about 20 women huddling in a circle under an outdoor tent, eager to learn about strength training despite the rainy weather.
“What are three common weaknesses in endurance athletes I see in the gym?” she asks them.
The group shouts out guesses. The first two are easy. Glutes! Adductors!—Chisholm agrees.
What’s the third one? Hip flexors? They’re up there, but there is something more important, Chisholm says.
This is the last session on the last day of FeistyFest, a three-day movement and educational festival for women held in September in Breinigsville, Pennsylvania, and none of the previous groups guessed the third one correctly, Chisholm says, before revealing the answer: “Power explosiveness!”
You can think of your explosive power as those first couple of seconds of your movement, the initial burst, Chisholm says. You’re recruiting fast-twitch muscle fibers, which quickly contract and generate high force, and activating your nervous system, which fires signals to your muscles at a high speed to help you coordinate complex movements.
“Injuries don’t happen when you’re just simply running forward often,” Chisholm says. When she sees them happen most? While moving laterally—“when you have to move quickly or in a different direction.” And that’s where explosive power comes in to help.
When you run, your body absorbs two to three times your body weight, which puts a lot of pressure on your joints and ligaments. Explosive power helps you control those forces safely and efficiently, while also improving speed, stride efficiency, and joint resilience.
Let’s start with the bad news: a 47-year Swedish study from 2025 published in the Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle concluded that explosive power peaks in women at 19 and in men at 27. That’s when your body starts losing its first line of defense against sudden physical stressors, and you become more injury-prone.
The good news? “We can train that, so your body is prepared to absorb the impact,” Chisholm says.
How to Train Explosive Power
Explosive power complements strength training, building on it. While strength training is all about the maximum amount of force a muscle can generate, explosive power helps you apply that power as quickly as possible.
Especially if you’re new to training your explosive power, adding one or two movements to your strength training session to start and slowly building up from there is the way to go, Chisholm says. “It could lead to injury if you do too much too fast, versus the actual goal that we want from it: to help with injury prevention,” she explains. “It’s really demanding, it’s hard on our body, and so we want to train it in lower reps.”
Besides how much, when you train explosive power also matters—you want to prime your body with explosive work before you get into strength. “When we want to train and get better at the explosive and power work, we need that fresh nervous system,” Chisholm says.
Chisholm is an ultrarunner, but she also used to play basketball, where agility and explosive power are essential and require training. Blending these two experiences, as a trainer, she programs athletic-style workouts that always include explosive power-focused moves in strength sessions. She starts with three Rs.
- Readiness: This is your warmup. You prepare your body for the session and activate muscles you’re going to use in the workout.

T-Bills Yield Up to 4.45%. Why Would Retirees Choose Dividend Stocks?
Treasury bills are paying rates that beat several household-name dividend stocks right now, but the retiree who chases that yield without reading the fine print may find their income cut in half before the decade ends.
As of October 23, 2026, Treasury bills paid average yields of 4% on the 4-week bill, 4.17% on the 13-week, 4.35% on the 26-week, and 4.45% on the 52-week. Every one of those rates is higher than the published dividend yields on three of the long-tenured income stocks in this comparison. Even so, a higher starting yield says only part of the story for a retiree who needs income for the next 20 years.
How a Treasury Bill Pays, and Why Your Rate Resets at Every Rollover
A Treasury bill is a short-term loan to the U.S. government. The Treasury sells bills at a discount or at par (face value), and when the bill matures, you receive the full face value. The difference between what you pay and what you get back is your interest. TreasuryDirect explains that for bills, “interest” is the difference between what you paid and the face value you get when the bill matures. Bills pay nothing along the way. You collect everything when the bill matures.
Bills come in 4-, 6-, 8-, 13-, 17-, 26-, and 52-week terms, with a $100 minimum purchase. The 4-week through 26-week bills auction weekly, and the 52-week bill auctions every four weeks. Your rate is fixed at auction and stays fixed only until the bill matures. When it does, you get your principal back and have to buy a new bill at whatever rate the next auction sets. That is reinvestment risk, and for retirees who live on rolling bills, it is the main risk they carry.
Rates have already moved in both directions within a year. The Federal Reserve’s target range tops out at 4.00% as of October 25, 2026. It was 4.25% a year earlier, fell to 3.75% from December 10, 2025 through September 15, 2026, and returned to 4% on September 16, 2026. Bill yields move with it.
The 52-week yield was 4.49% on October 14 and 4.45% on October 23. Someone rolling 4-week bills will get a new rate about a dozen times a year. Someone holding a 52-week bill locks in one rate for the year and carries all the rollover risk at a single date.
Government backing has limits that retirees should understand. The full faith and credit of the United States backs payment at face value at maturity. It does not protect the market price if you sell it before it matures. If rates rise after you buy, you can sell early for less than you paid. That price risk is small on a 4-week bill and increases with longer maturities.
Treasury notes, the longer-dated version, pay a fixed coupon for years and swing more in price. Treasuries are also securities, so FDIC deposit insurance doesn’t apply. And government backing does nothing for buying power. Consumer prices rose 0.6% from August in the September 2026 CPI reading. The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ research index for Americans 62 and older rose 0.5% over the same month.

Procurement teams budgeting for agentic rollouts are facing a specific, uncomfortable reality: the meter is going in, but the price is still a blank space. Salesforce has told customers it will soon charge for every call an agent makes to its platform, and for anyone trying to forecast what that costs, the newest row on the company's rate card – the one that will meter external agent calls – reads "TBA."
In a document published September 17, 2026, Salesforce set a November target for a new billing model under its Headless Toolkit. The mechanic is plain: every successful call a registered agent makes to Salesforce, whether it arrives over Model Context Protocol (MCP) or a direct API, is metered as one Headless Platform Interaction (HPI) and tracked through the company's Digital Wallet.
Worth stating plainly: agentic usage is not metered today. The multipliers for this usage type have not been announced, and Salesforce says it will give 30 days' notice when a numerical multiplier is added and metering begins. Traditional, non-agentic integration pricing stays exactly as it is – the model targets agentic traffic only, which is exactly why the registration step is the part to watch.
Registration is where the clocks start. Customers who purchase on or after September 17, 2026 must register all agents that use Salesforce APIs within three months' notice from Salesforce that Agentic Identity is available; existing customers running agents on APIs register and migrate at renewal; and any use of a Salesforce MCP server requires registration within that same three-month notice window, for all customers. Each registered agent gets its own Platform identity with a narrower permission set – Salesforce's own framing is issuing the agent its own badge rather than lending it an employee badge. The deadlines attach to a notice nobody has received yet.
When metering goes live, the cost lands in production first. Sandboxes, scratch orgs, and Developer Edition orgs incur no HPI metering, so teams can build and test without drawing down Flex Credits. The first bill arrives when those agents move into active production.
We tried to read the per-call number directly: the HPI usage-type row did not render on the Salesforce rate card when we fetched it, so the figure comes from the "TBA" status in Salesforce's help documentation, not from a published price. That gap is named rather than smoothed.
The November change also lands on top of what our price-card audit found this week. In our published-price-card audit, four of the eight tracked enterprise agent platforms published no public enterprise-agent price at all – and Salesforce still carries the fullest card in the group, Flex Credits at $500 per 100,000 credits. The base rate is a real number; the multiplier that converts each HPI into credits is not. This is adjacent to, not the same as, the authorization question we published today: that piece argues who permits an agent to move money is the chargeable surface, while Salesforce's Agentic Identity registration is a concrete case where registration gates metering

JPMorgan Has Nearly $900 Million in Tokenized Funds on Ethereum and Solana. Which Chain Benefits More?
JPMorgan just parked nearly $900 million in tokenized funds across Ethereum and Solana, but the fine print reveals one chain got a much bigger piece of the deal than the headlines suggest.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM | JPM Price Prediction) has made headlines by placing nearly $900 million in tokenized funds on both Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) and Solana (CRYPTO: SOL). A tokenized fund is an investment fund whose shares exist as tokens on a blockchain, allowing them to trade around the clock.
According to Sentora data, the JPMorgan OnChain Liquidity-Token Money Market Fund (JLTXX) holds about $792 million across both networks, while the My OnChain Net Yield Fund (MONY) holds an estimated $103.1 million on Ethereum alone.
In just one week, JPMorgan took two significant steps. On October 19, 2026, Kinexys, the bank’s blockchain unit, introduced its JPM Coin deposit token (JPMD) to Ethereum. Shortly after, on October 22, J.P. Morgan Asset Management launched MONY and JLTXX on Solana. However, despite these announcements, both cryptocurrencies saw declines: ETH fell to $2,333, down 2.1% for the week, while SOL dropped to $101, down 1.5%.
What JPMorgan Put on Ethereum and Solana, Product by Product
JLTXX is a U.S.-registered government money market fund that invests cash in short-term government debt and passes interest earnings directly to investors. JPMorgan designed it so that stablecoin issuers can hold reserves in JLTXX tokens under the GENIUS Act, a federal stablecoin law. JPMorgan first launched JLTXX on Ethereum in May.
MONY, by contrast, is a private placement regulated under the SEC’s Rule 506(c), meaning only high-net-worth individuals can invest. JPMorgan rolled this fund out in December 2025. Both funds operate through Morgan Money, JPMorgan’s cash management platform, allowing investors to subscribe and redeem, then receive tokens at a designated blockchain address. Retail traders cannot purchase these tokens on exchanges.
Meanwhile, JPMD is a deposit token representing a dollar held in a JPMorgan bank account, enabling institutional clients to transact at any time. It initially launched on Base, the blockchain connected to Coinbase (NASDAQ: COIN), where Sentora reports a $1 million supply, but it is not yet available on Ethereum.
These tokenized funds bring in modest revenue compared to JPMorgan’s core businesses. Fees from these funds contribute to Asset & Wealth Management, which manages over $5.1 trillion in client assets, while payments revenue, including JPMD, grew 12% in the second quarter. Additionally, neither Sentora nor JPMorgan has disclosed how JLTXX’s $792 million is split between Ethereum and Solana, making it hard to say Solana has a significant share.
What JPMorgan’s Announcements Left Out
The announcements did not commit anyone to buy or hold ETH or SOL. When a tokenized fund moves its assets, it incurs small transaction fees known as gas. However, money market fund tokens mainly sit in a few institutional wallets, so they generate far less fee activity than stablecoin transfers or trading.

International Business Machines Corp. Chairman and CEO Arvind Krishna questioned enterprise spending on frontier artificial intelligence models, stating that open-weight alternatives now offer nearly equal performance at a fraction of the price.
CEO Asks 'Why Pay 10x More?'
Speaking during the company's third-quarter 2026 earnings call, Krishna outlined the shrinking performance gap between the industry's most advanced frontier large language models and alternative open models. Krishna stated that open-weight models now run at 10% to 25% of the token cost of frontier models.
"Our computation is that for an average large enterprise, you can get going with maybe two or three racks, which is not a huge amount of infrastructure, but it gives you the ability to run those open-weight models. Currently, anywhere from 25% to 10% of the token cost of the frontier models. That is very attractive given that they're now 90% as effective," he said.
Krishna noted that in late 2024, open models scored significantly lower on benchmarks than frontier models, but the gap has narrowed to where alternate models are now about 90% as effective.
"It's a simple question for any enterprise," Krishna stated. "Would you like something that's 10% of the cost if it's 90% as good as the best, or do you want to pay that 10 times higher cost?"
Sovereign AI and Data Control
Krishna said the economics of open-weight models are converging with another major enterprise trend: sovereign AI. Companies increasingly want to keep sensitive data, logs and model activity under their own control, fueling demand for on-premises and private AI infrastructure.
For most daily enterprise tasks, such as summarizing emails, answering customer calls, or examining contracts, Krishna stated these cheaper alternative models are sufficient.
Krishna's remarks accompanied IBM's third-quarter financial results, where the company reported $17.1 billion in total revenue. IBM Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer Jim Kavanaugh reported a 9% acceleration in software revenue.
Additionally, Kavanaugh noted a 10% growth in transaction processing, driven by the company's mainframe software.
Validating management's earlier claims that second-quarter mainframe softness was merely a timing issue with slipped deals, technology analyst Patrick Moorhead posted on X that the previous quarter's drop was an "aberration."
The stock was 4.64% lower in overnight trading. It has declined 10.85% over the last year, down 15.11% year-to-date, but up 8.42% over the last month. The stock closed up 3.94% at $251.464 on Wednesday.
Benzinga's Edge Stock Rankings indicate that IBM maintains a strong price trend in the short term but a weak trend in the long and medium terms, with a poor value score.
